title: English Vocabulary 3 · Units 101
description: Curated American and British English spelling, lexical equivalents, regional usage and potentially confusing meanings.
sourceNotice: Prepared from the user-supplied book for personal study. Vocabulary targets follow source topics and exercise vocabulary; all teaching examples and notes are newly written, and original exercises, extended passages and illustrations are not reproduced.

audit.scope: Teaching sections A–D, vocabulary and spelling tables, illustrations, exercises 101.1–101.6 and the relevant answer-key entries checked for lexical and contextual coverage.
audit.pronunciation: British English IPA is supplied selectively where confidently known. Longer phrases and American-specific pronunciations with uncertain exact forms have empty IPA rather than guessed transcriptions. No recordings are bundled.
audit.languagePolicy: All content is in English except Brazilian Portuguese translations in pt.
audit.reviewMethod: Manual review of source pages and answer key; review of meaning, spelling, regional labels, sentence examples, IDs and static JSON/audio-target checks. The real VocabLab importer and browser audio were not executed.
audit.limitations: No live application import, TTS or speech-recognition test was performed. Empty audio denotes no bundled recording.

units.title: Unit 101 — US English
units.source: Vocabulary study targets from published reference material; Unit 101. Page information, if available, is retained in sourceAudit.
learningObjectives: Recognise frequent differences between American and British English vocabulary, grammar and spelling.
Choose appropriate American or British terms for transport, streets, household objects and everyday activities.
Recognise words with different meanings across varieties, including pants, vest, bill and wash up.
Avoid misunderstanding floor numbers in buildings and common travel expressions across varieties.

sectionsChecked: A: English in the USA; grammar and seasonal terms
B: American English spelling; spelling pairs and exceptions
C: US words and their British equivalents; travel, street and home tables
D: Different meanings; clothes, restaurant payment, washing up and floor numbering

items.example: We drove through New England in the fall to see the changing leaves.
items.note: AmE for the season called autumn in BrE; not the verb meaning to drop.

items.example: The university term begins in early autumn.
items.note: The usual BrE term for the season Americans commonly call fall.

items.example: We're planning to visit our cousins on the weekend.
items.note: AmE typically uses on the weekend; at the weekend is more typical in BrE.

items.example: I often catch up on reading at the weekend.
items.note: BrE commonly uses at the weekend; AmE commonly prefers on the weekend.

items.example: The color of the interface changes when you select dark mode.
items.note: Standard AmE spelling; colour is the standard BrE spelling.

items.example: The colour of the new curtains matches the walls.
items.note: Standard BrE spelling; AmE drops the u and writes color.

items.example: The new research center opened near the university.
items.note: Standard AmE -er spelling; BrE normally uses centre.

items.example: The museum is in the centre of the old town.
items.note: Standard BrE -re spelling; AmE normally uses center.

items.example: I didn't realize that the meeting had been moved to Friday.
items.note: Usual AmE -ize spelling; realise is common in BrE, where -ize is also accepted by some style guides.

items.example: She began to realise how much the course had helped her.
items.note: Common BrE -ise spelling; American English normally uses realize.

items.example: She keeps her jewelry in a small wooden box.
items.note: AmE spelling; BrE writes jewellery. Usually uncountable.

items.example: The shop sells handmade jewellery from local artists.
items.note: BrE spelling; AmE writes jewelry. Usually uncountable.

items.example: Could you do me a favor and review this email?
items.note: AmE spelling with -or; BrE writes favour.

items.example: Could you do me a favour and check these figures?
items.note: BrE spelling with -our; AmE writes favor.

items.example: The driver was hospitalized after the accident.
items.note: Common AmE spelling with -z-; hospitalised is common in BrE.

items.example: She was hospitalised for several days after the operation.
items.note: BrE spelling with -s-; AmE normally writes hospitalized.

items.example: A new movie theater is opening near the shopping center.
items.note: AmE phrase and spelling; BrE normally says cinema and spells theatre with -re.

items.example: We stopped to get gas before driving into the mountains.
items.note: AmE term for petrol; outside this context, gas can mean a gaseous substance.

items.example: The car consumes less gasoline than the older model.
items.note: Full AmE form of gas in the vehicle-fuel sense; BrE normally says petrol.

items.example: The petrol station was closed when we arrived.
items.note: BrE vehicle fuel; AmE normally uses gas or gasoline.

items.example: A delivery truck blocked the narrow road for several minutes.
items.note: AmE common term; BrE generally uses lorry for a large road vehicle.

items.example: A lorry carrying furniture stopped outside the building.
items.note: BrE term for a large goods vehicle; AmE generally uses truck.

items.example: Passengers should collect their baggage after customs.
items.note: Common in AmE, but also used in BrE, particularly for air travel; luggage is broadly used in BrE. Uncountable.

items.example: We left our luggage at the hotel before sightseeing.
items.note: Common BrE term; baggage is common in AmE and air-travel contexts. Uncountable.

items.example: Cyclists should not block the sidewalk outside the school.
items.note: AmE term; BrE normally uses pavement for the pedestrian path beside a road.

items.example: The children waited on the pavement for the bus.
items.note: BrE pedestrian path; AmE pavement often means the hard surface of a road or walkway.

items.example: Drivers must stop when pedestrians enter the crosswalk.
items.note: AmE; BrE uses zebra crossing for a crossing marked with stripes.

items.example: We used the zebra crossing near the library.
items.note: BrE for a striped pedestrian crossing; AmE generally says crosswalk.

items.example: There was a long line outside the concert venue.
items.note: In the waiting-person sense, AmE generally uses line; BrE often uses queue.

items.example: Please join the queue at the ticket office.
items.note: Common BrE noun or verb for waiting in a line; AmE often says line.

items.example: They took a two-week vacation in California.
items.note: AmE normally says vacation for a holiday trip or time off; BrE often says holiday.

items.example: We're going on holiday to Portugal next month.
items.note: BrE term for a vacation; in AmE, holiday often means a public celebration or day off.

items.example: The parking lot was full by nine in the morning.
items.note: AmE; BrE normally says car park.

items.example: The hospital has a multi-storey car park.
items.note: BrE; AmE normally says parking lot.

items.example: I put the toolbox in the trunk before leaving.
items.note: In AmE car vocabulary, the rear luggage compartment; BrE calls it the boot.

items.example: The suitcases were too large to fit in the boot.
items.note: BrE car luggage compartment; AmE calls it the trunk.

items.example: The mechanic opened the hood to inspect the battery.
items.note: AmE car front cover; BrE calls it the bonnet.

items.example: There was steam coming from under the bonnet.
items.note: BrE car front cover; AmE calls it the hood.

items.example: The freeway was congested during the evening rush hour.
items.note: An AmE high-speed road; often similar in function to a BrE motorway.

items.example: We took the interstate to travel between the two cities.
items.note: An AmE road that is part of the US Interstate Highway System; not simply every road crossing a state border.

items.example: The coach joined the motorway just outside the city.
items.note: BrE major high-speed road, broadly comparable to an AmE freeway.

items.example: She booked a one-way trip because her return date was uncertain.
items.note: AmE travel expression; BrE commonly refers to a single ticket.

items.example: Could I have a single ticket to Oxford, please?
items.note: BrE ticket for travel in one direction; AmE commonly says one-way ticket.

items.example: A round trip costs less than buying two separate tickets.
items.note: AmE for a journey out and back; BrE often uses return journey or return ticket.

items.example: I bought a return ticket so I wouldn't need to pay again later.
items.note: BrE for a ticket covering the outward and return journeys; AmE says round-trip ticket.

items.example: The railway car had comfortable seats and large windows.
items.note: AmE term; BrE may use railway carriage. In the US, railroad car is also common.

items.example: We found an empty railway carriage near the end of the train.
items.note: BrE term for a railway vehicle carrying passengers; AmE uses railway car or railroad car.

items.example: The subway is often faster than driving across Manhattan.
items.note: AmE underground urban railway; BrE commonly says the underground or the Tube in London.

items.example: We took the underground to reach the museum.
items.note: BrE, particularly London's underground railway; AmE usually says subway.

items.example: Please take the garbage out before you go to work.
items.note: AmE for waste; BrE commonly says rubbish.

items.example: The cleaner emptied the trash at the end of the day.
items.note: AmE for rubbish or waste; garbage and trash often overlap.

items.example: The bins are overflowing with household rubbish.
items.note: BrE for garbage or trash; also figuratively means nonsense.

items.example: Take the elevator to the fourth floor.
items.note: AmE; BrE normally says lift.

items.example: The lift is out of order, so we'll take the stairs.
items.note: BrE building elevator; in AmE lift usually has other senses.

items.example: Use an eraser if you make a mistake in pencil.
items.note: AmE; BrE calls this a rubber. In AmE, rubber may refer to a condom, so the context matters.

items.example: The pupil used a rubber to correct the drawing.
items.note: BrE stationery sense; AmE uses eraser. The word has other meanings in both varieties.

items.example: They rented an apartment near the university campus.
items.note: Common AmE term; BrE often uses flat.

items.example: Her flat is on a quiet street near the station.
items.note: Common BrE dwelling noun; AmE commonly says apartment.

items.example: There is a large closet next to the bedroom door.
items.note: AmE commonly refers to a built-in storage space; BrE often uses wardrobe for clothes storage.

items.example: The new wardrobe has enough room for all our coats.
items.note: BrE term for clothes storage, often a piece of furniture; an AmE closet is typically built in.

items.pt: quintal; área externa de uma casa
items.example: The children played in the yard after lunch.
items.note: AmE outdoor space around a home; a BrE garden is often the closest everyday equivalent.

items.example: They grow vegetables in the garden behind the house.
items.note: BrE often refers to the whole private outdoor area; AmE garden more often implies an area with plants.

items.example: We closed the drapes to block the afternoon sun.
items.note: AmE, especially for substantial fabric curtains; BrE generally says curtains.

items.example: The curtains kept the room cool throughout the day.
items.note: Common BrE term for window hangings; AmE also uses curtains alongside drapes.

items.example: Keep a flashlight near the door in case of a power cut.
items.note: AmE portable battery-powered light; BrE normally says torch.

items.example: He used a torch to look behind the wardrobe.
items.note: BrE portable light; an AmE torch often suggests a flame rather than a flashlight.

items.example: We ordered burgers with French fries for lunch.
items.note: AmE term; BrE often says chips for thicker fried potato pieces, but the styles can differ.

items.pt: batatas fritas em palitos ou tiras
items.example: The café serves fish and chips every Friday.
items.note: BrE fried potato pieces; in AmE, chips usually refers to crisp, thin snack slices.

items.example: She used Scotch tape to seal the paper envelope.
items.note: Common AmE brand-derived name for clear adhesive tape; BrE commonly uses Sellotape.

items.example: Could you pass me the Sellotape to wrap this present?
items.note: Common BrE brand-derived name for clear adhesive tape; AmE often says Scotch tape.

items.example: He bought a chocolate chip cookie from the bakery.
items.note: AmE cookie; BrE often uses biscuit. A US biscuit is a different kind of baked item.

items.example: She offered us a biscuit with our tea.
items.note: BrE usually means a sweet or savoury crisp baked snack; AmE biscuit commonly refers to a soft bread-like roll.

items.example: The shop sells candy near the checkout.
items.note: AmE general term for sweets; BrE uses sweets.

items.example: The children chose some sweets after the meal.
items.note: BrE; AmE typically calls these candy.

items.example: Excuse me, where is the bathroom?
items.note: AmE can refer to a toilet room even when no bath is present; BrE may say toilet.

items.example: The restroom is at the end of the corridor.
items.note: Polite AmE term for a public toilet; BrE generally uses toilet or WC.

items.example: Is there a public toilet near the bus station?
items.note: Common BrE term for the room or fixture; AmE often prefers restroom for a public facility.

items.example: The parents packed extra diapers for the journey.
items.note: AmE; BrE generally uses nappy.

items.example: We need to change the baby's nappy before leaving.
items.note: BrE; AmE generally uses diaper.

items.example: She bought a new pair of pantyhose for the ceremony.
items.note: AmE term for close-fitting legwear; BrE generally uses tights. Usually treated as a mass noun.

items.example: She wore thick tights under her skirt in winter.
items.note: BrE word for pantyhose; also used for thicker leg coverings.

items.example: In the US office, everyone wore smart pants and a collared shirt.
items.note: AmE pants are outer trousers; in BrE pants often means underpants.

items.example: He packed three clean pairs of pants for the weekend away.
items.note: In BrE, pants usually means underwear; in AmE, pants means trousers.

items.example: These trousers are too long and need shortening.
items.note: BrE for the outer garment called pants in AmE; plural in form.

items.pt: camiseta regata usada como roupa de baixo
items.example: He wore a cotton vest beneath his shirt on the cold morning.
items.note: BrE vest can mean an undershirt; AmE usually calls that an undershirt.

items.example: He wore a tailored vest with his suit.
items.note: AmE vest means the garment BrE commonly calls a waistcoat.

items.example: She bought an extra undershirt for the winter trip.
items.note: AmE term for the clothing BrE may call a vest.

items.example: He wore a grey waistcoat under his jacket at the wedding.
items.note: BrE for the sleeveless formal garment AmE calls a vest.

items.example: He put a spare pair of underpants in his overnight bag.
items.note: Underpants is understandable in both varieties; BrE also commonly uses pants.

items.example: Could we have the check when you're ready, please?
items.note: In an AmE restaurant, the check is the amount to pay; BrE normally calls it the bill.

items.example: We asked for the bill after finishing dinner.
items.note: In BrE restaurants, bill is usual; AmE often uses check.

items.pt: cédula de dinheiro; nota de papel-moeda
items.example: The cashier gave me two twenty-dollar bills in change.
items.note: AmE bill refers to a banknote; BrE usually says note.

items.example: He paid for the tickets with a ten-pound note.
items.note: BrE banknote; AmE usually says bill.

items.example: I'll wash up while you put the leftovers in the fridge.
items.note: In BrE, wash up often means wash the dishes after a meal.

items.example: Please wash up before we sit down to eat.
items.note: In AmE, wash up often means wash your hands or face; BrE may interpret it as washing dishes.

items.example: The reception desk is on the ground floor of the building.
items.note: In BrE, the level at street level is the ground floor; this corresponds to the first floor in many US buildings.

items.pt: primeiro andar no inglês americano; térreo no contexto brasileiro
items.example: The main entrance is on the first floor, right beside the street.
items.note: In typical US usage, first floor is the street-level floor; BrE calls that the ground floor.

items.example: The accountant's office is on the first floor above reception.
items.note: In BrE, first floor is one level above the ground floor, unlike typical AmE usage.

items.pt: segundo andar na contagem americana; um andar acima do térreo
items.example: Her office is on the second floor, one flight of stairs up.
items.note: In typical AmE usage, second floor is one level above street level; BrE calls it the first floor.

items.example: The meeting room is on the second floor, two flights above reception.
items.note: In BrE, second floor is two levels above the ground floor; in AmE it is typically one level above street level.
